source.title_on_document: The Impact of Generative AI Dependence on University Students' Creativity: The Mediating Role of Critical Thinking and the Moderating Role of Thinking Orientation

supplement.holds: Scale items (Tables S1-S4), priming statements (S5-S6), thinking-orientation manipulation check items (S7), CAT scoring rubrics (S8), and experimental task instructions for Studies 2 and 3. The document lists no extra statistics there; all reported statistics are in the main text.

paper_design_summary: Three studies with Chinese university students. Study 1 is a survey (N = 142) that correlates self-reported generative-AI dependence with self-reported creativity. Study 2 (N = 132) randomly assigns students to a high-dependence condition (ChatGPT answers used strictly in a priming phase, then ChatGPT ideas adopted directly in an Alternative Uses Task) or a low-dependence condition (no tools in the priming phase, then ChatGPT used only as a supplementary reference in the same AUT); trained raters score creativity with the Consensual Assessment Technique. Study 3 (N = 160) is a 2 x 2 design crossing an AI-dependence manipulation (trust game with AI investment advice) with a thinking-orientation prime, followed by the same AUT and rating.

assignment.what_was_assigned: Nothing; self-reported AI dependence, critical thinking, and creativity measured in one survey
assignment.quote: Study 1 aimed to preliminarily examine the relationship between generative AI dependence and university students' creativity, as well as the mediating role of critical thinking, through a cross-sectional survey design.

participants.who: University students (including graduate students) with generative AI usage experience; 63 males, 79 females; mean age 24.32 (SD 2.15)
participants.quote: A total of 142 university students (including graduate students) with generative AI usage experience were recruited via online platforms (63 males, 79 females; mean age = 24.32, SD = 2.15) from Qufu Normal University

ai_tool.name_model: Generative AI in general (no tool assigned)
ai_tool.how_used: Self-reported dependence on generative AI for academic tasks (3-item scale, Tang et al. 2023)

task.description: Survey only; no creative task. Creativity is a 6-item self-report scale (adapted from Akpur 2020).

outcomes.name: Self-reported creativity (6-item general creativity scale)
outcomes.question: none
outcomes.measure_detail: 6 items, alpha = 0.87, 5-point Likert; the paper says the scale 'captures self-perceived creative capacity across domains rather than performance on a specific creative task' (p. 3). Listed only to document why Study 1 does not qualify.

contrasts.reported: r = -0.20, p = 0.019; total effect B = -0.22, SE = 0.09, p = 0.019, 95% CI [-0.40, -0.04]; direct effect B = -0.07, SE = 0.11, p = 0.52; indirect effect via critical thinking -0.15, Boot SE = 0.06, 95% CI [-0.34, -0.10]
contrasts.locator: p. 4, Table 1 and Mediation analysis paragraph

studies.label: Study 2 (AI dependence manipulation, AUT with ChatGPT)

assignment.what_was_assigned: High vs low generative-AI dependence: instructions for using ChatGPT in a priming phase and in the scored creativity task
assignment.quote: A total of 132 university students (including graduate students; 51 males, 81 females) were recruited and randomly assigned to either the high-dependence group (n = 66) or the low-dependence group (n = 66).

arms.name: High AI dependence
arms.description: Phase 1: strictly used ChatGPT-generated answers for math calculation, text summarisation, and English translation, told 'the answers provided by the AI are optimal'. Phase 2 (AUT): used ChatGPT and was instructed to directly adopt the creative solutions ChatGPT generated.

arms.name: Low AI dependence
arms.description: Phase 1: same tasks done independently with no external tools (no calculators, translation apps, search engines, or AI). Phase 2 (AUT): used ChatGPT only as a supplementary reference and completed final solutions independently.

participants.exclusions: None reported. All between-group tests are reported with t(130), consistent with all 132 analyzed (p. 6, Table 2).
participants.who: University students including graduate students; 51 males, 81 females
participants.country: China (the paper states all participants came from a single institution, p. 12; Study 1 names Qufu Normal University)
participants.quote: A total of 132 university students (including graduate students; 51 males, 81 females) were recruited and randomly assigned

ai_tool.how_used: Both arms used ChatGPT during the scored AUT. High-dependence arm adopted ChatGPT's ideas directly (close to ideas_supplied); low-dependence arm used ChatGPT as a supplementary reference and wrote its own final solutions (open_chat with an independence instruction). The arms also differed in a prior priming phase (ChatGPT answers vs no tools).

task.description: Alternative Uses Task framed as a 'creative competition': generate as many innovative uses as possible for a tennis racket and a water pipe.

outcomes.name: Creativity index (CAT, mean of three raters on novelty, appropriateness, fluency)
outcomes.question: with_ai
outcomes.measure_detail: Consensual Assessment Technique: three trained psychology graduate students, blind to condition, scored each response on novelty, appropriateness, and fluency on 7-point scales; ICC = 0.86; mean of the three raters' scores is the creativity index (p. 6). The paper calls it 'expert-rated creativity' (p. 9). Sub-dimension scores are not reported separately. Critical thinking and self-efficacy are self-report scales and are not listed as outcomes.

contrasts.reported: Creativity: High AI Dependence 4.78 (0.66) vs Low AI Dependence 5.20 (0.53), n = 66 per group; t(130) = 4.03, p < 0.001, Cohen's d = 0.70 (d reported as positive for low minus high). Mediation: total effect c = -0.42, direct c' = -0.02, indirect ab = -0.40, bootstrap 95% CI [-0.70, -0.14].
contrasts.locator: p. 6, Section 3.3 Creativity performance and Table 2; p. 5 (n per group)

studies.label: Study 3 (2 x 2: AI dependence x thinking orientation, AUT)

assignment.quote: A total of 160 university students (including graduate students; 68 males, 92 females) were recruited and randomly assigned to one of four experimental conditions

arms.description: Trust game: instructed to exercise autonomous judgment; then rated statements that process matters more than outcomes; then AUT

arms.name: High AI dependence / process-oriented

participants.quote: low AI-dependence/outcome-oriented (n = 41), low AI-dependence/process-oriented (n = 39), high AI-dependence/outcome-oriented (n = 40), and high AI-dependence/process-oriented (n = 40).

eligibility.reason: Study 2 randomly assigns 132 students (66 per arm) to two ChatGPT configurations on an Alternative Uses Task (adopt ChatGPT's ideas directly vs use ChatGPT only as a reference), and blind trained raters score creativity of the AUT responses with CAT (pp. 5-6). This is an ai_design contrast with no no-AI arm in the scored task; the contrast also bundles a priming phase that differs in AI use (ChatGPT answers vs no tools). Study 3 (N = 160) is randomized but its AI manipulation is a trust game with unspecified AI advice, and AI availability during its AUT is stated only by reference to Study 2, so its criterion 1 is less clear. Study 1 is a survey with self-reported creativity and does not qualify.

one_line_finding: Students told to adopt ChatGPT's AUT ideas directly scored lower on rater-scored creativity than students told to use ChatGPT only as a reference (4.78 vs 5.20, t(130) = 4.03, d = 0.70; p. 6, Table 2), and in Study 3 the high-dependence deficit appeared under both thinking orientations (d = 1.95 and 5.09; p. 9).
open_questions: Study 3: was ChatGPT available during the Phase 3 AUT, and were the Study 2 adopt/reference instructions repeated? The paper says only that the task was 'identical to the AUT used in Study 2' (p. 8).
Study 3: is the 'AI investment advice' in the trust game generative AI? Not stated (p. 7).
Study 3: lab or online setting is not stated; lab_rct is coded by analogy to Study 2, which states a laboratory room with an experimenter present (p. 5).
Which arm counts as treatment in an ai_design contrast here: neither arm is a plain default. This form codes high dependence as treatment and low dependence as control.
Should a contrast that also differs in a prior priming phase (ChatGPT answers vs no tools, Study 2 Phase 1) be coded as ai_design or flagged as a bundled manipulation?
notes: Internal inconsistencies worth checking at extraction. (1) Study 2 Figure 3 (p. 7) shows paths 0.41***, -1.09**, and -0.38*** (0.06), while the text (p. 6) reports a = -0.40, b = 1.01, c = -0.42, c' = -0.02. (2) Study 1 Figure 2 (p. 4) shows -0.24***, 0.64***, 0.03 and (-0.13*), while the text reports total B = -0.22 and direct B = -0.07. (3) Study 3 simple effects for creativity use t(77) in the outcome-oriented condition, whose cells hold 41 + 40 = 81 people (expected df 79); the power paragraph says 40 per cell (p. 7). (4) The text calls the process-oriented creativity gap 'substantially attenuated' yet reports d = 5.09 vs 1.95 under outcome orientation; the raw gaps are 1.15 vs 1.53 (p. 9). (5) Table 4 Model 3 marks AI dependence B = -1.54 with ** although B/SE = 0.13 is far larger. (6) Study 3 manipulation check means (6.06, 4.95) exceed the 5-point range of the Tang scale used in Study 1; the scale range for Studies 2-3 is not stated. Critical thinking and self-efficacy in Studies 2 and 3 are self-report mediators and are not listed as outcomes. No diversity outcome is reported. The candidates.json note says 'GenAI conditions without stated random assignment'; the full text does state random assignment in Studies 2 and 3.
